---
title: "Quiz: generative adversarial networks"
---

Short questions on the generator, the discriminator and the game between them. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. $D(x)$ is the discriminator's probability that $x$ is real.

---

**Q1.** What does the generator of a GAN receive as input, and what does it never see?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Follow the arrows: where do real images go?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Random noise $z$ (for example 128 numbers from $\mathcal N(0, 1)$). It never sees a real image: it only gets the gradient of the discriminator's verdict on its own outputs.
:::

---

**Q2.** At some $x$, real data have density 0.3 and generated samples density 0.1. What is the best discriminator's output there?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$D^* = p/(p + q)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$0.3/(0.3 + 0.1) = 0.75$: three of every four points seen there are real.
:::

---

**Q3.** The generator has become perfect. What does the best discriminator output, and what is its loss $-\log D(\text{real}) - \log(1 - D(\text{fake}))$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$p = q$ everywhere.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$D = \tfrac12$ everywhere, and the loss is $-\ln\tfrac12 - \ln\tfrac12 = 2\ln 2 = 1.386$. The discriminator can do no better than guessing.
:::

---

**Q4.** Early in training the discriminator rates the generated samples $D(G(z)) = 0.02$. Compare the push on the generator from the original loss $\log(1 - D)$ and from the non-saturating loss $-\log D$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The derivatives with respect to the discriminator's logit are $-D$ and $-(1 - D)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
0.02 against 0.98: the non-saturating loss pushes 49 times harder, exactly when the generator is still bad. The original loss saturates.
:::

---

**Q5.** True or false: during GAN training, the generator's loss should go down steadily, as in ordinary training.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each loss is measured against an opponent who is also learning.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
False. A better discriminator raises the generator's loss even when the generator improves. In the demo both losses hover around $\ln 2$ and $2\ln 2$ at the end. GAN losses are not a progress bar; look at the samples and at distribution metrics ([next unit](../gan-training/lec.qmd)).
:::

---

**Q6.** Name two things a VAE gives you that a GAN does not, and one thing a GAN does better.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Think of the encoder and of the training objective.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A VAE has an encoder (image → code) and a likelihood bound (the ELBO), so it can score how typical an image is. A GAN produces much sharper samples.
:::

---

**Q7.** *(math)* Show that the best discriminator for fixed $p$ and $q$ is $D^* = p/(p + q)$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Maximise $p\log D + q\log(1 - D)$ at each $x$ separately.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The derivative with respect to $D$ is $p/D - q/(1 - D)$; it is zero at $p(1 - D) = qD$, i.e. $D = p/(p + q)$. The second derivative $-p/D^2 - q/(1 - D)^2 < 0$, so it is a maximum.
:::
